claim: Human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells have significantly larger horizontal extension (463.17±119.48 µm) compared to rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (324.79±80.58 µm).
source: measurements on 3D reconstructions based on randomly selected, electrophysiologically recorded, and biocytin-filled human (n=30) and rat (n=30) L2/3 cortical pyramidal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) show significant differences in the horizontal (463.17±119.48 vs 324.79±80.58 µm, t-test: p=1.687 × 10–6)
evidence: Supported by measurements on 3D reconstructions of 30 human and 30 rat neurons with statistical significance (p=1.687 × 10–6)

claim: Human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells have significantly larger vertical extension (542.58±146.89 µm) compared to rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (409.99±102.69 µm).
source: measurements on 3D reconstructions based on randomly selected, electrophysiologically recorded, and biocytin-filled human (n=30) and rat (n=30) L2/3 cortical pyramidal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) show significant differences in the horizontal (463.17±119.48 vs 324.79±80.58 µm, t-test: p=1.687 × 10–6) and vertical extensions (542.58±146.89 vs 409.99±102.69 µm, t-test: p=0.00013)
evidence: Supported by measurements on 3D reconstructions of 30 human and 30 rat neurons with statistical significance (p=0.00013)

claim: Human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells have significantly longer total dendritic length (9054.94±3699.71 µm) compared to rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (5162.68±1237.71 µm).
source: measurements on 3D reconstructions based on randomly selected, electrophysiologically recorded, and biocytin-filled human (n=30) and rat (n=30) L2/3 cortical pyramidal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) show significant differences in the horizontal (463.17±119.48 vs 324.79±80.58 µm, t-test: p=1.687 × 10–6) and vertical extensions (542.58±146.89 vs 409.99±102.69 µm, t-test: p=0.00013), and in the total dendritic (9054.94±3699.71 vs 5162.68±1237.71 µm, t-test: p=7.203 × 10–7)
evidence: Supported by measurements on 3D reconstructions of 30 human and 30 rat neurons with statistical significance (p=7.203 × 10–7)

claim: Human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells have significantly longer apical dendritic length (4349.76±1638.39 µm) compared to rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (2592.15±818.26 µm).
source: measurements on 3D reconstructions based on randomly selected, electrophysiologically recorded, and biocytin-filled human (n=30) and rat (n=30) L2/3 cortical pyramidal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) show significant differences in the horizontal (463.17±119.48 vs 324.79±80.58 µm, t-test: p=1.687 × 10–6) and vertical extensions (542.58±146.89 vs 409.99±102.69 µm, t-test: p=0.00013), and in the total dendritic (9054.94±3699.71 vs 5162.68±1237.71 µm, t-test: p=7.203 × 10–7) and apical dendritic length (4349.76±1638.39 vs 2592.15±818.26 µm, t-test: p=1.638 × 10–6, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by measurements on 3D reconstructions of 30 human and 30 rat neurons with statistical significance (p=1.638 × 10–6)

claim: There is no significant difference in synaptic latencies between human (1.111±0.306 ms, n=17) and rat (1.126±0.378 ms, n=19) pyramidal cell-to-pyramidal cell connections.
source: We did not find significant differences in synaptic latencies between human and rat PC-to-PC connections (rat: 1.126±0.378 ms, rat: n=19, human: 1.111±0.306 ms, n=17, Mann-Whitney test: p=0.949).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from synaptically connected cell pairs with statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test: p=0.949)

claim: The minimal intersomatic distance in synaptically connected pyramidal cell pairs is significantly larger in humans (402.12±74.757 µm) compared to rats (259.7±58.8 µm).
source: Consequently, we found that the minimal intersomatic distance (the sum of the shortest axonal and dendritic paths) in each synaptically connected PC-to-PC pair was significantly smaller in rats compared to humans (rat: 259.7±58.8 µm, human: 402.12±74.757 µm, Mann-Whitney test: p=0.009, Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by anatomical measurements from reconstructed synaptically connected cell pairs (n=6 rat, n=5 human) with statistical significance (p=0.009)

claim: Given similar synaptic latencies but different signal propagation distances, membrane potentials (APs and/or EPSPs) are likely to propagate faster in human pyramidal cell-to-pyramidal cell connections.
source: Given that similar synaptic latencies accompany different lengths for signal propagation in the two species, membrane potentials (APs and/or EPSPs) are likely to propagate faster in human PC-to-PC connections.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the combination of similar latencies and longer distances in humans

claim: There is no significant difference in the propagation speed of action potentials in axons between rats (0.848±0.291 m/s, n=8) and humans (0.851±0.387 m/s, n=9).
source: We found no significant difference in the propagation speed of APs in the axons of rats and humans (rat: n=8, 0.848±0.291 m/s vs. human: n=9, 0.851±0.387 m/s, two-sample t-test: p=0.282, Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by simultaneous somatic and axonal recordings with statistical analysis (two-sample t-test: p=0.282)

claim: The propagation speed of simulated EPSPs in dendrites is significantly faster in human (0.093±0.025 m/s) compared to rat (0.074±0.018 m/s) layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Left, simulated EPSP propagation speed in rat and human cells (rat: 0.074±0.018 m/s vs. human: 0.093±0.025 m/s, two-sample t-test: p=0.004).
evidence: Supported by dual dendritic-somatic recordings with simulated EPSP injections (n=24 each species) with statistical significance (p=0.004)

claim: The propagation speed of backpropagating action potentials in dendrites is significantly faster in human (0.344±0.139 m/s, n=62) compared to rat (0.233±0.095 m/s, n=46) layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: We found that the propagation speed was, on average, ~1.47 fold faster in human (rat: 0.233±0.095 m/s vs. human: 0.344±0.139 m/s, Mann-Whitney test: p=6.369 × 10–6, Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by simultaneous somatic and dendritic recordings with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney test: p=6.369 × 10–6)

claim: There is a significant correlation between forward propagating simulated EPSP speed and backpropagating AP speed (r=0.396, p=0.0053).
source: In addition, we found correlation between forward propagating sEPSP speed and back propagating AP speed (Pearson correlation coefficient, r=0.396, p=0.0053, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis of experimental data from 48 cells where both measurements were performed

claim: Human pyramidal cells have more depolarized resting membrane potential (–64.30±7.28 mV) compared to rat pyramidal cells (–70.49±5.78 mV).
source: In line with previous studies, human PCs in our dataset had more depolarized resting membrane potential (rat: –70.49±5.78 mV, human: –64.30±7.28 mV, Mann-Whitney U test: p=7.37 × 10–6, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U test: p=7.37 × 10–6)

claim: There is no significant difference in average somatic input resistance between rat (59.56±21.86 MΩ, n=46) and human (71.375±65.485 MΩ, n=62) layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: but the average somatic input resistance were not significantly different in the two species (rat: 59.56±21.86 MΩ, n=46, human: 71.375±65.485 MΩ, n=62, Mann-Whitney test: p=0.347, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements with statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test: p=0.347)

claim: HCN channel densities are higher in human compared to rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-modulated (HCN) channel densities were shown to be higher in human compared to rat layer 2/3 PCs and were shown to be instrumental in more depolarized resting membrane potentials and in larger sag potentials in response to hyperpolarization in the human (Kalmbach et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Kalmbach et al., 2018

claim: ZD7288 application did not significantly decrease backpropagating AP propagation speed in rat pyramidal cells (control: 0.163±0.054 m/s, ZD7288: 0.149±0.057 m/s, n=9).
source: Drug administration did not significantly decrease bAP propagation speed in rat PCs (control: 0.163±0.054 m/s, ZD7288: 0.149±0.057 m/s, n=9, two-way ANOVA with repeated measures and Tukey HSD (Honestly Significant Difference) post-hoc comparison: p=0.9, Figure 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments with ZD7288 (h-channel blocker) and statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA: p=0.9)

claim: ZD7288 application did not significantly decrease backpropagating AP propagation speed in human pyramidal cells (control: 0.322±0.073 m/s, ZD7288: 0.268±0.066 m/s, n=8).
source: and in human PCs (control: 0.322±0.073 m/s, ZD7288: 0.268±0.066 m/s, n=8, two-way ANOVA with repeated measures and Tukey HSD post-hoc comparison: p=0.329, Figure 3B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments with ZD7288 and statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA: p=0.329)

claim: Human dendrites maintained higher backpropagating AP propagation speed compared to rat dendrites even after h-channel blockage with ZD7288.
source: The human dendrites maintained a higher bAP propagation speed in response to h-channel blockage (two-way ANOVA with repeated measures and Tukey HSD post-hoc comparison: p=0.003).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments comparing species after ZD7288 treatment with statistical significance (p=0.003)

claim: Species-dependent density differences of HCN channels in pyramidal apical dendrites do not by themselves explain the propagation speed differences between human and rat.
source: These results suggest that the species-dependent density difference of HCN channels of pyramidal apical dendrites do not by themselves explain the propagation speed differences between the two species.
evidence: Based on inference from the ZD7288 pharmacological experiments showing maintained species differences after h-channel blockade

claim: Blockage of voltage-gated Na+ channels, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and NMDA receptors significantly reduced backpropagating AP propagation speed in rat pyramidal cells (control: 0.199±0.053 m/s, drug: 0.076±0.03 m/s).
source: The speed of back propagation of membrane potential signals in dendrites with blocked regenerative events by the pharmacological cocktail was significantly reduced in rat samples compared to the drug-free control (rat control: 0.199±0.053 m/s, rat TTX/CdCl2/AP5: 0.076±0.03 m/s, two-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD post-hoc comparison: p=0.024, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments with TTX, CdCl2, and AP5 with statistical significance (two-way ANOVA: p=0.024)

claim: Blockage of voltage-gated Na+ channels, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and NMDA receptors significantly reduced backpropagating AP propagation speed in human pyramidal cells (control: 0.395±0.14 m/s, drug: 0.184±0.061 m/s).
source: and was significantly lower in human samples as well (human control: 0.395±0.14 m/s, human TTX/CdCl2/AP5: 0.184±0.061 m/s, two-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD post-hoc comparison: p=0.001, Figure 3E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments with TTX, CdCl2, and AP5 with statistical significance (two-way ANOVA: p=0.001)

claim: There is no significant difference in specific membrane capacitance between rat (1.092±0.14 µF/cm2, n=20) and human (0.987±0.196 µF/cm2, n=19) layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: We found no significant difference in the Cm between the human and rat L2/3 PCs (rat: 1.092±0.14 µF/cm2 n=20; human: 0.987±0.196 µF/cm2 n=19, two-sample t-test: p=0.0615, Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by nucleated patch recordings with statistical analysis (two-sample t-test: p=0.0615)

claim: There is no significant difference in membrane thickness between human (4.271±0.873 nm, n=213) and rat (4.122±0.779 nm, n=151) dendritic structures.
source: We measured the membrane thickness of dendritic structures with transmission electron microscopy both in human and rat samples (Figure 4D and E) and detected no significant differences between the two species (human: 4.271±0.873 nm, n=213 from n=3 patient; rat: 4.122±0.779 nm n=151 from n=3 rat, Mann-Whitney test: p=0.212, Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy measurements with statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test: p=0.212)

claim: Specific membrane capacitance is not the key determinant of the higher signal propagation speed in human pyramidal cells.
source: Based on these experiments it seems that not the specific membrane capacitance is the key determinant of the higher signal propagation speed in human cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of significant differences in specific membrane capacitance and membrane thickness between species

claim: The mean diameter of dendrites is significantly thicker in human (2.272±0.584 µm, n=62) compared to rat (2.032±0.413 µm, n=46) pyramidal cells.
source: We found that the mean diameter of dendrites was thicker in human (2.272±0.584 µm, n=62) compared to the rat (2.032±0.413 µm, n=46, two-sample t-test: p=0.019, Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy measurements of dendrite thickness with statistical significance (two-sample t-test: p=0.019)

claim: The mean dendritic diameter between recording sites is correlated with the speed of backpropagating action potentials.
source: Moreover, in samples where we acquired both dendrite thickness and bAP signal propagation velocity, we found that the mean dendritic diameter between the recording sites was correlated with the speed of backpropagating APs (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of experimental data combining morphological and electrophysiological measurements

claim: EPSP latency in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (2.45±0.2 ms, n=5) is significantly shorter than in rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (3.3±0.3 ms, n=4) within the experimental range of dendritic recordings (27-289 µm).
source: For this experimental range of recordings, EPSP velocity ranged between 0.04–0.08 m/s in humans versus 0.03–0.05 m/s in rats. EPSP latency ranged between 0.1–4.7 ms in humans versus 0.4–6.5 ms in rats. These findings demonstrate significantly faster EPSP propagation in humans compared to rats (average latency in humans: 2.45±0.2 ms, n=5; in rats: 3.3±0.3 ms, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.03.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling of 5 human and 4 rat reconstructed neurons with uniform cable parameters, with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.03)

claim: EPSP velocity in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (0.08±0.005 m/s, n=5) is significantly faster than in rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (0.05±0.006 m/s, n=4) within the experimental range of dendritic recordings.
source: Average velocity in humans: 0.08±0.005 m/s, n=5; in rats: 0.05±0.006 m/s, n=4; Mann-Whitney U-test: p=0.02. See Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling with uniform cable parameters with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U-test: p=0.02)

claim: After normalizing distance in cable units and time in membrane time constant units, EPSP velocity remains significantly larger and latency shorter in human compared to rat pyramidal cells.
source: However, albeit such normalization, the velocity is still larger and the latency is shorter in human (compare insets in Figure 6D and E to Figure 6A and B, respectively. In this case, the average latency in humans: 0.16±0.01 τ, n=5; in rats: 0.22±0.02 τ, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.02. The average velocity in humans: 2.55±0.11 λ/τ, n=5; in rats: 1.73±0.29 λ/τ, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling with normalized parameters showing statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.02 for both latency and velocity)

claim: The basal tree membrane area in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (23,621±7735 µm2, n=5) is significantly larger than in rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (9127±2759 µm2, n=4).
source: Quantifying the total membrane area confirms that the basal tree in human is significantly larger than in rats (in humans: 23,621±7735 µm2, n=5; in rats: 9127±2759 µm2, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.02, see Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by quantification of membrane area from reconstructed neurons with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.02)

claim: Replacing the basal tree of human neurons with rat basal tree (creating 'hybrid cells') diminishes the inter-species differences in EPSP latency and velocity.
source: To examine the impact of impedance load, we computationally substituted the basal tree of human neurons with the basal tree of rat and vice versa (creating 'hybrid cells'). This substitution diminished the inter-species differences in latency and velocity (both in the original units and after normalizing the distance and time in units of λ and τ, respectively).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling experiments with hybrid cell manipulations

claim: In hybrid cell models where all cells have the basal tree of 'Rat4', there is no significant difference in EPSP latency between human (3.42±0.5 ms, n=5) and rat (3.2±0.2 ms, n=4) neurons.
source: This resulted in a significant reduction in EPSP velocity in the human neurons, diminishing the differences in signal latency/velocity between humans and rats (average latency in humans: 3.42±0.5 ms or 0.23±0.03 in units of τ, n=5; in rats: 3.2±0.2 ms, 0.21±0.01 in units of τ, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.7 for both ms and τ units.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling of hybrid cells with statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.7)

claim: In hybrid cell models where all cells have the basal tree of 'Rat4', there is no significant difference in EPSP velocity between human (0.06±0.005 m/s, n=5) and rat (0.05±0.005 m/s, n=4) neurons.
source: Average velocity in humans: 0.06±0.005 m/s or 1.86±0.1 λ/τ, n=5; in rats: 0.05±0.005 m/s or 1.8±0.1 λ/τ, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.73 for m/s units and p=0.66 for λ/τ units. See Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling of hybrid cells with statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.73 for m/s, p=0.66 for λ/τ)

claim: The large conductance load imposed by the large basal dendritic tree at the soma is the key factor responsible for accelerated EPSP propagation in human cortical dendrites.
source: Experimentally-based detailed biophysical models have shown that the key factor responsible for the accelerated EPSP propagation in human cortical dendrites is the large conductance load imposed at the soma by the large basal dendritic tree.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling experiments including hybrid cell manipulations and statistical analyses

claim: Specific membrane resistivity (Rm) is larger in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells compared to rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: We found that Rm is larger in humans and Cm is smaller in humans (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by fitting cable parameters to experimental data from individual neurons (Table 1 shows mean human Rm: 17,120 Ωcm2 vs mean rat Rm: 11,304 Ωcm2)

claim: Specific membrane capacitance (Cm) is smaller in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells compared to rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: We found that Rm is larger in humans and Cm is smaller in humans (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by fitting cable parameters to experimental data from individual neurons (Table 1 shows mean human Cm: 0.70 µF/cm2 vs mean rat Cm: 1.11 µF/cm2)

claim: The membrane time constant (τ=Rm*Cm) is statistically similar between human and rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Yet the membrane time constant (τ=Rm*Cm) is statistically similar in the two species (Table 2 and see Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by calculation from fitted cable parameters (Table 2 shows mean human τ: 11.9 ms vs mean rat τ: 12.1 ms)

claim: With fitted cable parameters per cell, EPSP latency in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (2.3±0.4 ms, n=5) is significantly shorter than in rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (3.2±0.6 ms, n=4) within the experimental range.
source: For this experimental range of recordings, EPSP velocity ranged between 0.04–0.08 m/s in humans versus 0.03–0.05 m/s in rats. EPSP latency ranged between 0.1–4.7 ms in humans versus 0.4–6.5 ms in rats. These findings demonstrate significantly faster EPSP propagation in humans compared to rats (average latency in humans: 2.45±0.2 ms, n=5; in rats: 3.3±0.3 ms, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.03. Average velocity in humans: 0.08±0.005 m/s, n=5; in rats: 0.05±0.006 m/s, n=4; Mann-Whitney U-test: p=0.02. See Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling with per-cell fitted parameters with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.03)

claim: With fitted cable parameters per cell, EPSP velocity in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (0.085±0.009 m/s, n=5) is significantly faster than in rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (0.05±0.0085 m/s, n=4) within the experimental range.
source: average latency in humans: 2.3±0.4 ms, or 0.19±0.03 τ, n=5; in rats: 3.2±0.6 ms or 0.27±0.05 τ, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.03 for both ms and τ units. Average velocity in humans: 0.085±0.009 m/s or 2.5±0.4 λ/τ, n=5; in rats: 0.05±0.0085 m/s or 1.7±0.3 λ/τ, n=4; Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.03 for m/s and p=0.02 for λ/τ units. See Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Table 2).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling with per-cell fitted parameters with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U test: p=0.03 for m/s, p=0.02 for λ/τ)

claim: Physical distance of synapses from soma has the strongest effect on EPSP propagation latency among all factors analyzed.
source: Our analysis revealed the following ranking order: (1) physical distance of synapses from soma had the strongest effect; (2) species differences; (3) conductance load, as demonstrated by our 'hybrid cells' manipulation; (4) radii of the apical dendrite, affecting the cables' space constant, λ; and (5) the specific cable parameters, as revealed when using per-cell fitted parameters versus uniform cable parameters, was minimal.
evidence: Supported by generalized linear model (GLM) analysis without interaction terms and SHAP analysis

claim: Species differences have the second strongest effect on EPSP propagation latency among all factors analyzed.
source: Our analysis revealed the following ranking order: (1) physical distance of synapses from soma had the strongest effect; (2) species differences; (3) conductance load, as demonstrated by our 'hybrid cells' manipulation; (4) radii of the apical dendrite, affecting the cables' space constant, λ; and (5) the specific cable parameters, as revealed when using per-cell fitted parameters versus uniform cable parameters, was minimal.
evidence: Supported by generalized linear model (GLM) analysis without interaction terms and SHAP analysis

claim: Conductance load (as demonstrated by hybrid cells manipulation) has the third strongest effect on EPSP propagation latency among all factors analyzed.
source: Our analysis revealed the following ranking order: (1) physical distance of synapses from soma had the strongest effect; (2) species differences; (3) conductance load, as demonstrated by our 'hybrid cells' manipulation; (4) radii of the apical dendrite, affecting the cables' space constant, λ; and (5) the specific cable parameters, as revealed when using per-cell fitted parameters versus uniform cable parameters, was minimal.
evidence: Supported by generalized linear model (GLM) analysis without interaction terms and SHAP analysis

claim: The average membrane time constant of human and rat layer 2/3 pyramidal cells is similar at approximately 11 ms.
source: Our experimentally-based models showed that the average membrane time constant of the two species is similar (~11 ms).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling with fitted cable parameters (Table 2 shows human: 11.9 ms, rat: 12.1 ms)

claim: EPSPs arising in the apical dendrite at similar distances from the soma have significantly shorter latency in humans compared to rats.
source: Yet, EPSPs arising in the apical dendrite at similar distances from the soma have significantly shorter latency in humans.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results showing shorter latencies in humans within the experimental distance range

claim: The larger diameter of the apical trunk in humans is the primary factor contributing to shorter EPSP latency.
source: This results primarily from the larger diameter of the apical trunk in humans, but also from the difference in cable properties between the two species.
evidence: Based on inference from modeling results showing diameter effects and hybrid cell experiments

claim: The significantly larger basal tree in human layer 2/3 cells implies a larger conductance load at the soma, which enhances EPSP propagation velocity and reduces synaptic latency.
source: We show that the significantly larger basal tree in human L2/3 cells implies a larger conductance load there and as shown in Figures 6 and 8, this enhances EPSP propagation velocity and reduces synaptic latency to the soma (see also Agmon-Snir and Segev, 1993).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling experiments including hybrid cell manipulations and cited theoretical work

claim: The increased conductance load (increased sink) in human layer 2/3 neurons will enhance EPSPs originated in the basal tree as well, not specifically in the apical tree.
source: It is important to note that this increased conductance load (increased sink) in human L2/3 neurons (and probably also in other cortical neurons and other neuron types which are larger in human compared to rat) will enhance EPSPs originated also in the basal and not specifically in the apical tree.
evidence: Based on inference from the understanding of how conductance load affects signal propagation

claim: The membrane time constant τ is similar in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells of rodents and humans, implying preservation of coincidence detection capabilities of dendrites in both species.
source: Noteworthy here is that we found that the membrane time constant, τ, is similar in L2/3 PCs of rodents and human implying the preservation of coincidence detection capabilities of dendrites in both species.
evidence: Based on inference from the similar membrane time constants found in both species

claim: Soma-to-soma pyramidal cell synaptic latencies are similar in human and rodent, suggesting that compensatory mechanisms evolved together with alterations in dendritic structure.
source: Our observation that soma-to-soma pyramidal cell synaptic latencies are similar in human and rodent strongly suggest that compensatory mechanisms evolved together with alterations in dendritic structure such as increased thickness of dendritic segments in the human compared to segments equidistant from the soma in the rat.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings of similar latencies despite different morphologies

claim: Similar soma-to-soma latencies between presynaptic pyramidal cells and postsynaptic fast spiking interneurons were found in human and rat.
source: This finding is backed up by earlier experiments showing similar soma-to-soma latencies between presynaptic pyramidal cells and postsynaptic fast spiking interneurons in human and rat (Szegedi et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Szegedi et al., 2016

claim: Similar soma-to-soma latencies were found between human and mouse pre-and postsynaptic cells overall in the neocortex.
source: and between human and mouse pre-and postsynaptic cells overall in the neocortex (Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Campagnola et al., 2022

claim: Signals connecting pyramid-to-pyramid and pyramid-to-interneuron cell pairs have an evolutionally conserved latency.
source: Thus, it appears that signals connecting pyramid-to-pyramid and pyramid-to-interneuron cell pairs have an evolutionally conserved latency and compensation provided by dendritic structure seems precise.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings and cited literature showing similar latencies across species

claim: There is no indication of significant over/under-compensation and acceleration/deceleration of soma-to-soma propagation times based on available datasets.
source: Importantly, based on the datasets available, there is no indication of significant over/under-compensation and acceleration/deceleration of soma-to-soma propagation times.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing similar latencies without systematic deviations

claim: Precision in monosynaptic latencies across species is instrumental in keeping the timeframe relatively stable for circuit plasticity.
source: Precision in monosynaptic latencies across species is instrumental in keeping the timeframe relatively stable for circuit plasticity.
evidence: Based on inference from the importance of timing in plasticity mechanisms and the observed conservation of latencies

claim: Spike time dependent plasticity (STDP) is based on the relative timing of pre-and postsynaptic activity.
source: Spike time dependent plasticity (STDP) is based on the relative timing of pre-and postsynaptic activity (Caporale and Dan, 2008; Feldman, 2012; Markram et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on STDP

claim: Human neurons show a wide temporal STDP window with a reversed STDP curve compared to classic results detected in rodent brain.
source: Pioneering STDP studies in human neurons showed a wide temporal STDP window with a reversed STDP curve compared to classic results detected in rodent brain (Bi and Poo, 1998; Verhoog et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by Bi and Poo, 1998 and Verhoog et al., 2013

claim: Dendritic L-type voltage-gated calcium channels are important in human STDP rules.
source: Interestingly, dendritic L-type voltage-gated calcium channels were found important in human STDP rules (Verhoog et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Verhoog et al., 2013

claim: The faster backpropagating AP propagation in human pyramidal cells is compatible with the shifted STDP rule switch by allowing postsynaptic somatic action potentials to be generated later yet arriving to dendrites at the same time relative to presynaptic spikes.
